# tool reference

Every tool a session can hold, generated from `ronin.tools.registry.build_registry`.
The description text below each heading is the *exact* string sent to the model —
`Tool.describe()` renders it, in a fixed order (summary, when to use, when not to
use, worked examples), because a description that only says what a tool does gets
called in situations it should not be.

A session does not necessarily have all of these. `build_registry` gates each group
behind a dependency: no shell means no `bash`, no fetcher means no `web_fetch`. A
tool that is absent is invisible to the model, which is strictly better than one that
exists and always errors. `--mode plan` narrows the set further, to read-only tools
only, and re-derives that property from the specs rather than trusting a prompt.

`danger level` decides what the permission gate does with a call: `read_only` never
asks, and anything higher can be gated by a rule in `.ronin/settings.json`. See
[config.md](config.md).

13 tools, listed alphabetically.

| tool | danger level | approval by default |
|---|---|---|
| [`bash`](#bash) | destructive | yes |
| [`bash_output`](#bash_output) | read_only | no |
| [`edit`](#edit) | mutating | yes |
| [`glob`](#glob) | read_only | no |
| [`grep`](#grep) | read_only | no |
| [`ls`](#ls) | read_only | no |
| [`multi_edit`](#multi_edit) | mutating | yes |
| [`read`](#read) | read_only | no |
| [`task`](#task) | read_only | no |
| [`todo_write`](#todo_write) | read_only | no |
| [`web_fetch`](#web_fetch) | read_only | no |
| [`web_search`](#web_search) | read_only | no |
| [`write`](#write) | mutating | yes |

## bash

`danger_level` `destructive` (2 of 3) · `requires_approval` `true`

### arguments

| argument | type | required | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `command` | string | yes | The shell command to run. |
| `timeout` | integer | no | Seconds before the command is killed. Default 120. |
| `description` | string | yes | 5-10 words on what this does, shown in the approval prompt. |
| `run_in_background` | boolean | no | Return a handle immediately instead of waiting. For servers/watchers. |

### description, as the model receives it

```text
Run a shell command in a persistent bash session.

WHEN TO USE
Running tests, builds, linters, git commands, package managers — anything with a CLI. The session persists, so `cd` and `export` and an activated venv carry over to your next call; set up once and then work.

WHEN NOT TO USE
Do not use bash for searching or reading. Use the grep tool instead of `grep`/`rg` (it respects gitignore and caps output), the glob tool instead of `find`, the read tool instead of `cat`/`head`/`tail`, and the ls tool instead of `ls` — those calls are refused here. Interactive programs (vim, less, top) are refused too: there is no terminal, so they would hang. For a command that does not exit — a dev server, a file watcher — pass run_in_background=true and tail it with bash_output.

EXAMPLE
bash(command="uv run pytest tests/ -q", description="Run the test suite")
→ 309 passed in 3.25s
(exit 0)

EXAMPLE
bash(command="cd src && pwd", description="Move into src")
→ /repo/src  — and the next bash call still starts in /repo/src

EXAMPLE
bash(command="npm run dev", description="Start the dev server", run_in_background=true)
→ started in background: handle=bg_1. Tail it with bash_output(handle='bg_1')
```

## bash_output

`danger_level` `read_only` (0 of 3) · `requires_approval` `false`

### arguments

| argument | type | required | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `handle` | string | yes | The handle bash returned. |

### description, as the model receives it

```text
Read new output from a background command started by bash.

WHEN TO USE
Checking on something you launched with run_in_background=true: has the dev server come up, did the build finish, what did the watcher print. Each call returns only what is new since the last one.

WHEN NOT TO USE
Not for a command that already finished in the foreground — its output was in the bash result. Do not poll this in a tight loop; do other work and check back.

EXAMPLE
bash_output(handle="bg_1")
→ ready on http://localhost:3000
(still running)
```

## edit

`danger_level` `mutating` (1 of 3) · `requires_approval` `true`

### arguments

| argument | type | required | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | string | yes | File to edit. |
| `old_string` | string | yes | Exact text to replace, copied verbatim from the file. |
| `new_string` | string | yes | Replacement text. |
| `replace_all` | boolean | no | Replace every occurrence. Default false. |

### description, as the model receives it

```text
Replace an exact string in a file with another.

WHEN TO USE
Any change to an existing file. This is the default editing tool: it changes exactly what you name and provably leaves the rest alone.

WHEN NOT TO USE
Do not use it to create a file — use write. Do not guess at old_string; if the match fails, read the file and copy the text verbatim rather than trying a near-miss again. For several changes to one file, use multi_edit so they are all-or-nothing.

EXAMPLE
edit(path="src/app.py", old_string="timeout=30", new_string="timeout=60")
→ edited src/app.py (1 replacement)

EXAMPLE
edit(path="src/app.py", old_string="return None", new_string="return []")
→ REFUSED: old_string appears 4 times — extend it with surrounding lines, or pass replace_all=true
```

## glob

`danger_level` `read_only` (0 of 3) · `requires_approval` `false`

### arguments

| argument | type | required | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pattern` | string | yes | Glob such as "**/*.py" or "src/**/test_*.py". |
| `path` | string | no | Directory to search. Defaults to root. |

### description, as the model receives it

```text
Find files by name pattern, newest first.

WHEN TO USE
You know roughly what a file is called but not where it is: `glob(pattern="**/test_*.py")`. Newest-first ordering means the files someone touched recently — usually the relevant ones — come up top.

WHEN NOT TO USE
Not for searching file *contents* — that is grep. Not for listing one directory you already know the path of — that is ls, and it is cheaper.

EXAMPLE
glob(pattern="**/*.toml")
→ pyproject.toml
examples/models.toml
(2 files)
```

## grep

`danger_level` `read_only` (0 of 3) · `requires_approval` `false`

### arguments

| argument | type | required | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pattern` | string | yes | Regular expression (Rust regex). |
| `path` | string | no | File or directory to search. |
| `glob` | string | no | Restrict to matching files, e.g. "*.py". |
| `type` | string | no | File type, e.g. "py", "ts", "rust". |
| `mode` | string | no | content = matching lines, files = paths, count = per-file counts. |
| `-A` | integer | no | Lines of trailing context. |
| `-B` | integer | no | Lines of leading context. |
| `-C` | integer | no | Lines of context on both sides. |
| `-i` | boolean | no | Case-insensitive. |
| `-n` | boolean | no | Show line numbers. Default true. |
| `multiline` | boolean | no | Let the pattern span lines. |

### description, as the model receives it

```text
Search file contents with a regular expression.

WHEN TO USE
Finding where something is defined or used, which is most of exploring an unfamiliar codebase. Start with mode='files' to see which files are involved, then mode='content' with -C for the ones that matter.

WHEN NOT TO USE
Do not call grep through bash — this wraps ripgrep, respects gitignore, and returns capped output, none of which `bash grep -r` does. Do not use it to find files by *name*; that is glob.

EXAMPLE
grep(pattern="class \\w+Client", type="py", mode="files")
→ src/ronin/providers/anthropic.py
src/ronin/providers/openai_compat.py

EXAMPLE
grep(pattern="TODO", glob="*.py", mode="content", **{"-C": 2})
→ src/x.py:12:    # TODO: fix
(with two lines of context each side)
```

## ls

`danger_level` `read_only` (0 of 3) · `requires_approval` `false`

### arguments

| argument | type | required | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | string | yes | Directory to list. |
| `ignore` | array | no | Glob patterns to skip, e.g. ["*.pyc", "__pycache__"]. |

### description, as the model receives it

```text
List the contents of one directory.

WHEN TO USE
Orienting in a directory you have a path for — seeing what is at the root of a repo, or what is inside a package.

WHEN NOT TO USE
Not for searching. If you are looking for a file whose location you do not know, glob finds it in one call instead of several ls calls walking down. Do not use ls to explore a whole tree; it lists one level on purpose.

EXAMPLE
ls(path="src/ronin", ignore=["__pycache__"])
→ core/
providers/
tools/
__init__.py
demo.py
```

## multi_edit

`danger_level` `mutating` (1 of 3) · `requires_approval` `true`

### arguments

| argument | type | required | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | string | yes | File to edit. |
| `edits` | array | yes | Edits applied in order. |

### description, as the model receives it

```text
Apply several exact-string edits to one file, all or nothing.

WHEN TO USE
Two or more changes to the same file. Edits apply in order to an in-memory buffer, so a later edit sees the result of an earlier one — which is what you want when renaming a symbol and then changing a line that used it.

WHEN NOT TO USE
Not for a single change (use edit) and not across several files (call it once per file). If any edit in the list fails, none of them are written, so do not use it to make a best-effort batch of independent changes.

EXAMPLE
multi_edit(path="src/app.py", edits=[
  {"old_string": "def old_name(", "new_string": "def new_name("},
  {"old_string": "old_name(x)", "new_string": "new_name(x)", "replace_all": true}
])
→ edited src/app.py (2 edits, 4 replacements)
```

## read

`danger_level` `read_only` (0 of 3) · `requires_approval` `false`

### arguments

| argument | type | required | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | string | yes | File to read, absolute or relative. |
| `offset` | integer | no | 1-indexed line to start at. Use with limit for a big file. |
| `limit` | integer | no | How many lines to read. |

### description, as the model receives it

```text
Read a file from disk and return its contents with line numbers.

WHEN TO USE
Before editing anything — write and edit both need to know what is already there, and write refuses to overwrite a file you have not read. Also for reading config, tests, or any file a grep hit pointed you at.

WHEN NOT TO USE
Do not read a file you already read this session unless you changed it. Do not read a whole directory tree hoping to find something; use glob or grep to narrow first, then read the two or three files that matter. Do not use read to check whether a file exists — ls or glob answers that far cheaper.

EXAMPLE
read(path="src/main.py")
→ 1	import sys
     2	
     3	def main() -> None:

EXAMPLE
read(path="logs/big.log", offset=4000, limit=100)
→ lines 4000-4099 of a 50,000-line file
```

## task

`danger_level` `read_only` (0 of 3) · `requires_approval` `false`

### arguments

| argument | type | required | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `prompt` | string | yes | The complete task. The subagent sees nothing else — no history, no context — so state everything it needs. |
| `subagent_type` | string | yes | Which kind of subagent to spawn. |

### description, as the model receives it

```text
Spawn a subagent with fresh context; get back only its final answer.

WHEN TO USE
When answering means reading across many files and you want the conclusion, not the file dumps. The subagent's forty grep hits and eight reads cost its context, not yours. Also for independent work you can run while you do something else.

WHEN NOT TO USE
Not for a single lookup where you already know the file — read it yourself, a subagent is slower. Not for anything needing your conversation history: the subagent starts fresh and cannot see it. Not for work that must edit files, unless you spawn a type whose tool list includes editing.

EXAMPLE
task(prompt="Find every place we construct a ModelRequest and list file:line for each", subagent_type="explore")
→ 3 sites: providers/assembly.py:98, providers/bridge.py:81, providers/shim.py:412 — assembly.py is the only one callers should use.

AVAILABLE SUBAGENT TYPES
- explore: Read-only search across many files. Use when answering a question means sweeping a directory and you only want the conclusion. (tools: read, glob, grep, ls)
- summarize: Condense a file, a diff, or command output into the parts that matter. (tools: read, grep)
```

## todo_write

`danger_level` `read_only` (0 of 3) · `requires_approval` `false`

### arguments

| argument | type | required | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `todos` | array | yes | The complete list, every call. Not a delta. |

### description, as the model receives it

```text
Write or update your plan as a checklist the user can see.

WHEN TO USE
Any task with three or more steps, and any task where you will be working for a while. Write the plan before starting, then update it as you go: mark one item in_progress, complete it, move to the next. This is what keeps a long task coherent, and it is what the user reads to know you are still on the thing they asked for.

WHEN NOT TO USE
Not for a single-step task — a one-item checklist is noise. Not as a place to write notes or findings; the items are steps, and the plan should stay readable at a glance.

EXAMPLE
todo_write(todos=[
  {"content": "Read the failing test", "status": "completed"},
  {"content": "Fix the off-by-one in parse()", "status": "in_progress"},
  {"content": "Run the suite", "status": "pending"}
])
→ [x] Read the failing test
[~] Fix the off-by-one in parse()
[ ] Run the suite
(1/3 done)
```

## web_fetch

`danger_level` `read_only` (0 of 3) · `requires_approval` `false`

### arguments

| argument | type | required | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `url` | string | yes | The http(s) URL to fetch. |
| `prompt` | string | yes | What to extract. Be specific; this is all the extractor gets. |

### description, as the model receives it

```text
Fetch a URL and answer a question about it, without loading the page.

WHEN TO USE
You have a specific URL and a specific question: what does this changelog say changed in 3.0, what arguments does this API take, what is the error in this CI log. The page goes to a cheaper model and you get the answer.

WHEN NOT TO USE
Not for finding a page — that is web_search. Not when you need the page verbatim: the result is an extraction, so if exact wording matters say so in the prompt ('quote the relevant lines exactly'). Not for a localhost URL; curl it with bash instead.

EXAMPLE
web_fetch(url="https://example.com/CHANGELOG.md", prompt="What changed in version 3.0? List the breaking changes.")
→ 3.0 removed the sync client and renamed `timeout` to `timeout_s`. …
```

## web_search

`danger_level` `read_only` (0 of 3) · `requires_approval` `false`

### arguments

| argument | type | required | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `query` | string | yes | The search query. |

### description, as the model receives it

```text
Search the web and get back result titles, URLs and snippets.

WHEN TO USE
You need a page you do not have the URL for: current documentation, an error message someone else has hit, whether a library supports something. Follow up with web_fetch on the one or two results that look right.

WHEN NOT TO USE
Not for anything in this repository — grep is faster and actually correct. Not as a substitute for reading the code you already have. Snippets are advertising copy; do not answer from them without fetching the page.

EXAMPLE
web_search(query="ripgrep multiline mode flag")
→ 1. ripgrep guide — https://…  |  --multiline enables patterns spanning lines
```

## write

`danger_level` `mutating` (1 of 3) · `requires_approval` `true`

### arguments

| argument | type | required | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | string | yes | File to write. |
| `content` | string | yes | The complete new contents. |

### description, as the model receives it

```text
Write a file, replacing its entire contents.

WHEN TO USE
Creating a new file, or replacing one small enough that a full rewrite is clearer than a series of edits.

WHEN NOT TO USE
Do not use write to change part of an existing file — use edit, which cannot accidentally drop the parts you did not mention. Writing a file you have not read this session will be refused, because a full overwrite of something you have not seen destroys work you do not know about.

EXAMPLE
write(path="tests/test_new.py", content="def test_x():\n    assert True\n")
→ wrote tests/test_new.py (2 lines, 34 bytes)

EXAMPLE
write(path="src/existing.py", content="...")
→ REFUSED: src/existing.py exists and has not been read this session
```
